 Diapers Drew More Incident Reports Than Any Product Category Since 2011, Yet Regulators Have Never Announced a Recall
 Published Nov 20, 2026 2:00 PM EST 
 By
 Joseph James 
 Riccardo Milani | Hans Lucas | AFP via Getty Images 
 Share on Twitter 
 Share on Facebook 
 Share on WhatsApp 
 Diapers have drawn more incident reports to the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission than any other product category from 2011 through 2026, yet the CPSC has never announced a diaper recall or issued a diaper safety warning, a CBS News analysis of CPSC reports published Nov. 19 found.
 Much of that total comes from this year. The data include 735 reports involving Millie Moon diapers, most of them filed in 2026. Without 2026, diapers ranked fifth among product categories, with more than 300 reports from 2011 through 2025.
 For parents changing a baby six or more times a day, the gap between complaints and action leaves a hard choice at home. There is no official finding that any brand caused the rashes, and no official signal that the products are safe to keep using , either.
 Fifteen Years of Diaper Complaints
 Millie Moon reports climbed from 16 in April 2026 to 108 in May, according to CBS. Before this year, the high mark was 2025, with 95 diaper reports, 83 of them involving Huggies. In 2011, there were 77 reports involving Pampers.
 Parents describe rashes, redness, swelling, blisters, peeling, and what some called chemical burns. Consumer Reports counted more than 600 Millie Moon reports this year, with numerous reports describing medical treatment, including at least three emergency room visits. Several parents said their children had previously worn Millie Moon diapers without trouble.
 Consumer Reports urged parents to stop using the diapers while the cause is investigated and called on the company to recall them, NBC News reported . In its review, no other diaper brand came close to that level of incidents over the same period.
 Awareness also shaped the count. A Reddit user asked other parents about Millie Moon experiences in February, and another posted a link to the CPSC reporting site at the end of April, shortly before reports jumped, CBS found. That timing does not make the reports less real, but it shows how quickly a parent network can turn scattered complaints into a federal record.
 "We think the number of incidents, as well as the severity of the incidents, speak for themselves," Gabe Knight of Consumer Reports told CBS.
 Huggies maker Kimberly-Clark faces a separate class action, filed in November 2025, alleging that it changed the formula of its hypoallergenic diapers without telling consumers. The claims have not been proven in court.
 A Common Rash With Many Possible Causes
 Diaper rash is among the most common skin problems of infancy, and it can have many causes, which makes any single source hard to pin down. Moisture, friction, yeast, new foods, antibiotics, wipes, creams, and laundry products can all play a role.
 Incident reports on SaferProducts.gov are submitted by the public and are not verified as proof that a product caused harm. A large number of similar reports can be a meaningful safety signal, but it is not the same as a finding.
 The CPSC has faced this before. From April through August 2010, the agency received about 4,700 reports about diaper rash, most tied to Pampers Dry Max, and its review found no specific cause linking the diapers to the rashes. Procter & Gamble never recalled the product, though a later class action settlement paid $1,000 each to 59 parents and $400,000 toward pediatric skin health training.
 Company Statements and Regulatory Gaps
 Millie Moon told CBS that it went beyond routine testing and worked with seven independent organizations, and that "we have found no product-related cause of the reported reactions." It said skin-irritation complaints make up fewer than 0.1% of its diaper packs sold.
 Kimberly-Clark said its testing shows its diapers are safe and that they are made without parabens, elemental chlorine, natural rubber latex, phthalates, or fragrance.
 The CPSC said it is investigating the Millie Moon incidents but cannot comment on active investigations. The agency told CBS that earlier diaper investigations did not find enough justification for a substantial product hazard and that it is open to considering new rules.
 To force a recall, the CPSC must show a substantial product hazard. Unlike cribs, strollers, carriers, and nursing pillows , diapers have no dedicated federal safety standard. General rules for infant products require labeling with the maker, date, and batch, plus testing for contaminants such as lead, but not ingredient disclosure or standardized absorbency testing.
 Some states have moved on their own. California's AB1901 requires ingredient disclosure for children's diapers, and New York and Illinois have similar labeling laws. Sydney Swanson of the Environmental Working Group told CBS, "I think it's a space that we need more regulation." 
 Signs a Diaper Rash Needs Medical Care
 Most diaper rashes improve within a few days with frequent changes, time without a diaper, and a barrier cream. Parents should call a pediatrician for blisters, open or bleeding sores, peeling skin, pus, a rash that spreads beyond the diaper area, or a rash that does not improve after two to three days. A rash with fever, or a baby who is feeding poorly or unusually fussy, needs prompt attention.
 Parents who suspect a diaper can stop using it, switch to another brand while the skin heals, and keep the package, the lot or batch number, and photos of the rash. Those details help a clinician sort out the cause and make a report to SaferProducts.gov more useful to investigators.
 Steroid creams and other medicated products should be used only on a clinician's advice, since some are not meant for infant skin. Switching brands can also strain a budget, and local diaper banks may help families who cannot afford to replace a large supply.
 MedicalDaily will report if the CPSC announces findings, a warning, or any recall involving diapers.

 Key Questions Answered
 What did the CBS News analysis find? Diapers drew more CPSC incident reports than any other product category from 2011 through 2026, largely because of Millie Moon reports this year.
 Has any diaper ever been recalled? No. The CPSC has never announced a diaper recall or issued a diaper safety warning.
 What do the reports describe? Rashes, blisters, peeling, and what parents called chemical burns, sometimes requiring medical treatment.
 What does Millie Moon say? It says testing found no product-related cause and that complaints make up fewer than 0.1% of packs sold.
 When should a diaper rash be seen by a doctor? For blisters, open sores, pus, peeling, a spreading rash, fever, or no improvement after two to three days.
 How can parents report a problem? At SaferProducts.gov, ideally with the package's lot or batch number and photos.
